newsitem.title: KENYA: Drought-affected Kenya coffee retains high quality.
newsitem.headline: Drought-affected Kenya coffee retains high quality.

text.p: Kenya's drought-affected mild washed arabica coffee continues to attract high prices while the cup quality remains high, a senior official of the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) said at the weekend.

"When I saw the effect of the drought in March I was shocked, it's only the second time I've seen such a bad drought, and I expected the cup quality to be very poor," said Simeon Onchere, the CBK's London-based overseas representative.

"But up to now the quality of the coffee coming from the drought-affected areas has been surprisingly good, I am pleasantly surprised that the general feeling is that the cup quality is very good," Onchere told Reuters.
He said the cup quality was reflected in high prices for Kenya's premium mild-washed arabica coffee, which was selling above prices on the New York arabica market.

Onchere predicted that prices on the coffee auction in Nairobi on Tuesday would be higher than the general expectation, due to high competition on the world market for the high-quality coffees for the gourmet sector.

"The prices (on Tuesday) will be better than people expect because the competition at the moment is very stiff and people are starting to buy the top quality arabica coffee for Christmas now," Onchere said.
"The premiums are fetching prices above New York and...what is going to happen in the next year is that the top quality end of the market will continue to attract high prices," he said.

Kenya's coffee crop in the 1996/97 season has been badly affected by a severe drought which swept all of East Africa from late last year to around March this year and which has led to huge drops in original crop forecasts.

Kenya produces two coffee crops a year, the main and smaller mid crop, which is reaching the auction now. Onchere said the fly crop was seen at 20 to 30 percent lower than early predicted due to the drought, but was unable to give any figures.

"There is going to be a potential drop of anything between 20 and 30 percent of the fly-crop, but we don't know how much yet, the bags are currently being brought in from the farms and we are going to have the final count by the end of September."

Coffeee production in 1996/97 (October/September) is now estimated at just around 75,000 to 78,000 tonnes on account of drought compared to 97,575 tonnes in 1995/96 and 95,806 tonnes in 1994/95, according to official statistics.
Coffee stands third behind tourism and tea as a leading foreign exchange earner, government statistics show.
Kenya's share of world coffee trade is about 2.3 percent but its mild arabicas earn premiums well above world market rates.

Arabicas cover 176,500 hectares of land under coffee in Kenya while robustas account for just 1,000 hectares. Some 70 percent of the total hectarage under coffee is cultivated by 335,000 smallholders.
